title: F.W.R: Escort the King Into Castling
summary: Use the rook checks to escort the king down the board, then activate the untouched rook through the stipulated queenside castle.

nodes.question: How can White keep the king moving toward the first rank?
nodes.explanation: Rd6+ begins a forced staircase. The black pieces and pawns deny their own king room while White keeps the queenside castling right for the finish.

branches.title: Source staircase and the castling finish
commentary: Begin after ...Kd5 with both black rooks, bishop, queen and all remaining pawns intact. White’s queenside castling right is an explicit source stipulation.
Rd6+ cuts across the sixth rank and checks down the d-file. The black king has exactly one legal response.
Ke4 is forced. Black’s own c5 rook and d3 pawn help restrict the king; the checking rook covers the d-file.
Rd4+ checks along the fourth rank. The rook is protected by the white c3 pawn, so the king cannot capture it.
Kf3 is the only legal reply. Black’s d3 pawn blocks one escape, and White’s d2 pawn controls e3.
Rf4+ shifts the check onto the f-file. The bishop on h2 protects f4 along h2–g3–f4.
Kg2 is forced. White’s king and pawns control the neighboring squares that might otherwise let Black escape.
Rf2+ brings the rook to the second rank, checking Kg2 while denying the king a return up the f-file.
Kh1 is forced into the corner. White has preserved the unmoved king and a1 rook for the final activation.
O-O-O+ is legal under the source-stipulated right: e1, d1 and c1 are safe, and b1/c1/d1 are empty. The rook arriving on d1 checks along the first rank.
Qf1 is Black’s sole legal defense, interposing the queen between Rd1 and Kh1. The castle itself was check, not immediate mate.
Rdxf1# uses the rook that just castled to capture the blockading queen. The f2 rook remains on f2 and the h2 bishop controls g1, leaving the king no legal answer.

exercises.prompt: Why must the castling right remain in the position?
exercises.answer: The finish activates Ra1 with O-O-O+. Removing the stipulated right changes the legal moves and would invalidate this lesson.

exercises.prompt: Does castling itself end the game?
exercises.answer: No. Black can interpose Qf1. Rdxf1 is the actual mate, with the other rook still on f2.

startContext: Begin at 121 seconds after ...Kd5 in the complete sixteen-piece later diagram. The source explicitly stipulates White queenside castling; that right is preserved, not inferred from a still image. Every selected position is certified by a finite legal strategy ending in actual mate, retaining all pieces and checking every Black defense. This is castling-aware legal verification, not a Syzygy tablebase proof. The preceding queen sacrifice, knight capture and first rook checks remain unverified source context.
